learn.b: A budget is a plan for your money. You write down the money coming in (income) and the money going out (expenses). Example: if you earn $200 and spend $150, you have $50 left.
Needs are things you must have, like rent, food and transport. Wants are extras, like games or fancy sneakers. A good budget pays for needs first.
One simple plan is 50% of income for needs, 30% for wants and 20% for savings or paying off debt. It is a guide, not a law. You can change the numbers to fit your life.

qs.q: Which of these is a need?
qs.why: Housing is a basic need, while the others are wants.

qs.q: In the 50/30/20 rule, what share goes to savings or debt payments?
qs.why: The 20 in 50/30/20 is for savings and debt repayment.

qs.q: Your income is higher than your expenses. What do you have?
qs.why: Money left over after expenses is called a surplus.

qs.q: Why is it useful to track your spending?
o: To see where your money actually goes
qs.why: Tracking shows real habits so you can adjust your budget.

qs.q: Net income is the money you earn before taxes are taken out.
qs.why: Net income is what you keep after taxes; before taxes it is gross income.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
Put the budgeting steps in order

learn.b: An emergency fund is cash kept for surprises like a broken phone or a medical bill. Many experts suggest saving 3 to 6 months of basic expenses. Keep it in an easy-to-reach savings account.
Interest is money a bank pays you for keeping money with it. Simple interest uses only your starting amount (the principal). Example: 5% simple interest on $100 for one year is $5.
With compound interest, you earn interest on your principal and on the interest you already earned. Money grows faster over time. Starting early gives compounding more time to work.

qs.q: How much is a common emergency fund goal?
qs.why: Many experts suggest 3 to 6 months of basic expenses.

qs.q: You earn 5% simple interest on $100 for one year. How much interest is that?
What does compound interest mean?
o: Interest only on the starting amount
A fee for opening an account
Interest paid once at the end of life
Interest on both principal and past interest
qs.why: Compounding adds earned interest to the base that earns more interest.

qs.q: Which usually pays you interest?
qs.why: Banks pay interest on money held in savings accounts.

qs.q: Starting to save earlier usually lets compound interest grow your money more.
qs.why: More time means more compounding periods.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
$1,000 grows 10% a year, compounded. Order the balance from year 0 to year 3

learn.b: A credit score is a number that shows how likely you are to repay money you borrow. Paying bills on time is the biggest factor. Lenders use it to decide whether to lend to you and at what rate.
APR means annual percentage rate, the yearly cost of borrowing. If you do not pay your full statement balance, interest is added to what you owe. Credit limit is the most you can borrow on the card.
Debt is money you owe. Paying only the minimum keeps you in debt longer and costs more interest. Paying the full balance on time avoids card interest.

qs.q: What does a credit score mainly show?
o: How likely you are to repay debt
qs.why: It estimates your reliability as a borrower.

qs.q: How can you avoid credit card interest?
o: Pay the full statement balance by the due date
Use the card up to the limit
qs.why: Paying in full on time usually means no interest charged.

qs.q: What does APR stand for?
qs.why: APR is the yearly cost of borrowing as a percentage.

qs.q: Which action helps a credit score most?
qs.why: Payment history is a major scoring factor.

qs.q: Paying only the minimum on a credit card usually means paying more interest over time.
qs.why: The balance shrinks slowly, so interest keeps building.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
Order these borrowing costs from lowest to highest

learn.b: Net worth is what you own (assets) minus what you owe (liabilities). Example: $500 in savings and a $100 debt gives a net worth of $400.
Inflation is when prices rise over time. A bag of snacks that costs $2 today may cost more in ten years. Money kept only in cash buys less as time passes.
Insurance shares the risk of big losses. You pay a small premium, and the insurer pays for covered problems after your deductible. Clear goals help too: a good goal has an amount and a date.

qs.q: How do you calculate net worth?
qs.why: Net worth equals what you own minus what you owe.

qs.q: Which best describes inflation?
o: Prices generally rising, so money buys less
qs.why: Inflation is a general rise in prices.

qs.q: What is the main purpose of insurance?
o: To protect against large unexpected losses
qs.why: Insurance spreads the cost of big risks across many people.

qs.q: Which is the best savings goal?
o: Save $600 in 6 months by putting aside $100 monthly
qs.why: It has a clear amount, deadline and plan.

qs.q: A checking account is mainly designed for long-term growth of savings.
qs.why: Checking is for everyday spending; savings and investments are for growth.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
Put the steps to reach a savings goal in order
items: Set a goal amount and date

learn.b: A stock is a small piece of ownership in a company. If the company grows, the share price may rise. Some companies also pay dividends, a share of profit paid to owners.
A bond is a loan you give to a company or government. They pay you interest and return your money on a set date. Bonds are usually less risky than stocks.
Higher possible returns usually come with higher risk of losing money. Savings accounts are safer but grow slowly. Stocks can grow more but go up and down.

qs.q: What does owning a share of stock mean?
o: You lent money to a company
You own a small part of the company
qs.why: A stock is an ownership share.

qs.q: What is a bond?
o: A loan made to a company or government
qs.why: Bond buyers lend money and receive interest.

qs.q: Generally, higher potential returns come with what?
qs.why: Risk and return are linked.

qs.q: What is a dividend?
o: A share of profit paid to shareholders
qs.why: Some companies pay part of profits to owners as dividends.

qs.q: Owning a stock guarantees that you will make money.
qs.why: Stock prices can fall, so losses are possible.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
Order by typical risk, from lowest to highest

learn.b: Diversification means spreading money across many investments. If one falls, others may hold up. It is like not putting all your eggs in one basket.
An index fund holds the stocks in an index, like the S&P 500, which tracks 500 large US companies. An ETF is a fund that trades on an exchange like a stock. Both give instant diversification.
Funds charge an expense ratio, a yearly fee as a percent of your money. A 0.1% fee costs $1 a year on $1,000. Lower fees mean you keep more of your returns.

qs.q: What is diversification?
qs.why: Diversifying reduces the impact of any single investment failing.

qs.q: What does an index fund do?
o: Tracks a market index like the S&P 500
qs.why: Index funds copy the holdings of an index.

qs.q: What is an expense ratio?
o: A fund's yearly fee as a percent of assets
qs.why: It is the annual cost of owning the fund.

qs.q: How does an ETF trade?
o: On an exchange during the day like a stock
qs.why: ETF shares are bought and sold on exchanges.

qs.q: An index fund holds many stocks, so it is diversified.
qs.why: Owning many companies spreads risk.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
Order from least diversified to most diversified

learn.b: EPS is a company's profit divided by its number of shares. If a company earns $100 million and has 20 million shares, EPS is $5.
The P/E ratio is share price divided by EPS. A $50 stock with $5 EPS has a P/E of 10. It shows how much investors pay for each $1 of earnings.
Market cap is share price times the number of shares, the total value of a company. A bull market is rising prices, a bear market is falling prices.

qs.q: How is the P/E ratio calculated?
o: Price per share divided by earnings per share
qs.why: P/E equals price divided by EPS.

qs.q: A stock costs $50 and EPS is $5. What is the P/E ratio?
How do you calculate market cap?
o: Share price times number of shares
qs.why: Market cap is the total market value of all shares.

qs.q: What is a bear market?
o: A period of broadly falling prices
qs.why: Bear markets are marked by sustained price declines.

qs.q: Market capitalization is the total value of all of a company's shares.
qs.why: It equals share price times shares outstanding.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
Order company sizes by market cap, smallest to largest

learn.b: Time horizon is how long until you need the money. Volatility is how much prices swing up and down. Longer horizons give more time to ride out swings.
Dollar-cost averaging means investing a fixed amount at regular times, like $50 each month. You buy more shares when prices are low and fewer when high. It avoids trying to guess the best day.
Over time some investments grow faster, changing your mix. Rebalancing means adjusting back to your target mix. Risk tolerance is how much loss you can handle without panic.

qs.q: What is dollar-cost averaging?
o: Investing everything on the cheapest day
Investing a fixed amount at regular intervals
qs.why: It spreads purchases across time.

qs.q: What does volatility measure?
o: How much prices move up and down
qs.why: High volatility means big price swings.

qs.q: Why can a longer time horizon help investors?
o: There is more time to recover from dips
qs.why: Longer periods let markets recover from short-term drops.

qs.q: What is rebalancing?
o: Adjusting your investments back to a target mix
qs.why: It restores your intended proportions.

qs.q: Past performance guarantees future results.
qs.why: Past returns do not promise future returns.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
Put the steps of a simple investing plan in order
items: Set a goal and time horizon

learn.b: A blockchain is a shared digital record book. Transactions are grouped into blocks, and each block links to the one before it. This makes old records very hard to change.
Decentralized means no single company or government is in charge. Many computers, called nodes, each keep a copy of the ledger. They check each other's work.
Bitcoin was the first cryptocurrency, created by a person or group called Satoshi Nakamoto. It launched in 2009. Only 21 million bitcoin can ever exist.

qs.q: What is a blockchain?
o: A shared ledger of linked blocks of transactions
qs.why: Blocks of transactions are chained together in a shared record.

qs.q: Who created Bitcoin?
qs.why: Bitcoin was created under the name Satoshi Nakamoto.

qs.q: What does decentralized mean?
qs.why: Control is spread across many participants.

qs.q: What is the maximum supply of Bitcoin?
qs.why: Bitcoin's code caps supply at 21 million.

qs.q: One person can easily edit old records on a large blockchain.
qs.why: Changing old blocks would require redoing many linked blocks and beating the network.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
Put how a transaction is recorded in order
items: It is added to a block
The block is linked to the chain

learn.b: A public address is like an email address: you share it to receive crypto. A private key is like a password that allows spending. Never share your private key.
A seed phrase is a list of words that can restore your wallet. Anyone with it can take your funds. Write it down and keep it offline.
A hot wallet is connected to the internet, a cold wallet is offline. In a custodial wallet, like an exchange, a company holds the keys for you. In self-custody, you hold them yourself.

qs.q: What does a private key do?
qs.why: The private key proves ownership and signs transactions.

qs.q: What is a public address used for?
qs.why: You can share it so others can send you funds.

qs.q: Who should know your seed phrase?
qs.why: Anyone with the seed phrase can control your wallet.

qs.q: What is a cold wallet?
o: A wallet stored in a fridge
A wallet that is always online
qs.why: Cold storage is not connected to the internet.

qs.q: If you lose your private key and have no backup, you may lose access to your crypto permanently.
qs.why: No central company can reset it in self-custody.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
Order the steps for setting up a self-custody wallet
items: Install a wallet from the official source
Write your seed phrase on paper

learn.b: Consensus means the network agrees on which transactions are valid. Bitcoin uses proof of work, where miners use computer power to solve puzzles. The winner adds the next block.
In proof of stake, validators lock up coins as a stake. They are chosen to add blocks and can lose stake if they cheat. It uses much less energy than proof of work.
A smart contract is a program on a blockchain that runs automatically when conditions are met. Ethereum made them popular. Users pay a gas fee to process transactions.

qs.q: What do miners do in proof of work?
o: Solve computational puzzles to add blocks
Lock up coins as a stake
qs.why: Miners compete to solve puzzles and add the next block.

qs.q: What do validators do in proof of stake?
o: Lock up coins as stake to help add blocks
qs.why: Validators put coins at stake to earn the right to add blocks.

qs.q: What is a smart contract?
o: A program that runs automatically on a blockchain
qs.why: It executes code when set conditions are met.

qs.q: Which blockchain is best known for smart contracts?
qs.why: Ethereum popularized programmable smart contracts.

qs.q: Bitcoin uses proof of stake.
qs.why: Bitcoin uses proof of work.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
pairs: Solves puzzles in proof of work
Stakes coins in proof of stake

qs.q: Order these crypto events by year
items: Ethereum moves to proof of stake

learn.b: Crypto prices can rise or fall a lot in a short time. This is high volatility. Some stablecoins try to avoid this by tracking a steady asset like the US dollar.
Scammers promise guaranteed high returns, rush you, or ask for your seed phrase. Real projects never need your seed phrase. A rug pull is when creators abandon a project and take the money.
Crypto is used for payments, DeFi (financial services on blockchains) and NFTs (unique digital tokens). Transactions usually cannot be reversed. Laws about crypto differ by country.

qs.q: What is a stablecoin designed to do?
o: Keep a steady value tied to an asset
qs.why: Stablecoins aim to hold a stable value, such as one dollar.

qs.q: How would you describe crypto prices?
qs.why: Crypto prices often swing sharply.

qs.q: Which is a common scam red flag?
qs.why: No real investment can guarantee high returns.

qs.q: What is an NFT?
o: A unique digital token tied to a specific item
qs.why: NFTs are one-of-a-kind tokens on a blockchain.

qs.q: Crypto sent to the wrong address usually cannot be reversed.
qs.why: Blockchain transactions are generally final.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
Put a scam-spotting routine in order
items: Check if the sender is official

learn.b: Scarcity means resources are limited but wants are unlimited. Because of this, everyone must make choices. Even rich people have limited time.

Opportunity cost is the value of the next best thing you give up when you choose. If you spend Saturday at the beach instead of a paid shift, the shift is what you gave up. Every choice has a trade-off.
An incentive is something that motivates people to act, like a discount or a reward. People usually respond to incentives. Economics studies how people make choices with limited resources.

qs.q: What is scarcity?
qs.why: Scarcity is the gap between limited resources and unlimited wants.

qs.q: What is opportunity cost?
o: The value of the next best alternative you give up
The cost of making a good
qs.why: It measures what you sacrifice by choosing one option.

qs.q: What is an incentive?
qs.why: Rewards and costs push people toward certain behavior.

qs.q: What does economics study?
o: How people make choices with limited resources
qs.why: Economics is about choices under scarcity.

qs.q: Scarcity only affects poor people.
qs.why: Everyone faces limited time, money or resources.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
pairs: Giving up one thing for another

qs.q: Put the steps of a good decision in order

learn.b: Demand is how much buyers want at each price. The law of demand says that when price rises, quantity demanded falls. Supply is how much sellers offer, and when price rises, quantity supplied rises.
Equilibrium is the price where the amount buyers want equals the amount sellers offer. At that price there is no shortage and no surplus. Markets tend to move toward it.
If the price is below equilibrium, buyers want more than sellers offer: a shortage. If the price is above equilibrium, sellers have extra goods: a surplus. Prices then tend to adjust.

qs.q: According to the law of demand, if price rises, quantity demanded usually does what?
qs.why: Higher prices lead buyers to buy less.

qs.q: According to the law of supply, if price rises, quantity supplied usually does what?
qs.why: Higher prices encourage sellers to offer more.

qs.q: What is equilibrium?
o: The price where quantity supplied equals quantity demanded
qs.why: At equilibrium the market clears.

qs.q: What happens when price is below equilibrium?
qs.why: Buyers want more than sellers supply at the low price.

qs.q: A surplus happens when the price is set above equilibrium.
qs.why: Sellers offer more than buyers want at a high price.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
pairs: What buyers want at each price
What sellers offer at each price

qs.q: A toy becomes very popular. Order what happens next

learn.b: Elasticity shows how much quantity changes when price changes. Elastic demand means buyers react a lot, like for a luxury treat. Inelastic demand means buyers react little, like for salt.
Fixed costs do not change with how much you make, like rent. Variable costs change with output, like ingredients. Marginal cost is the extra cost of making one more unit.
Revenue is money from sales. Profit equals total revenue minus total cost. A firm often keeps producing while the extra revenue from a unit is more than its marginal cost.

qs.q: What does elastic demand mean?
o: Quantity demanded changes a lot when price changes
Quantity does not respond to price
qs.why: Elastic means buyers are very sensitive to price.

qs.q: Which good likely has the most inelastic demand?
qs.why: People need salt and have few substitutes, so price changes matter little.

qs.q: Which is a fixed cost for a bakery?
qs.why: Rent stays the same however many loaves are baked.

qs.q: How is profit calculated?
qs.why: Profit is what remains after costs.

qs.q: Marginal cost is the total cost of all units produced.
qs.why: Marginal cost is the extra cost of producing one more unit.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
Put the steps to find profit in order
items: Check if the result is positive

learn.b: In perfect competition there are many sellers of identical goods, so no one controls the price. A monopoly has one seller. An oligopoly has a few big firms, like some phone companies.
An externality is a cost or benefit that affects people who were not part of the deal. Pollution is a negative externality. A neighbor's beautiful garden can be a positive one.
A public good, like national defense or streetlights, is available to everyone and one person using it does not stop others. Private companies often will not provide them, so governments often do.

qs.q: What is a monopoly?
qs.why: Mono means one: a single seller controls the market.

qs.q: What is an oligopoly?
qs.why: Oligopolies are dominated by a small number of big firms.

qs.q: What is an externality?
o: A cost or benefit affecting people outside a deal
qs.why: Outsiders feel effects they did not choose.

qs.q: Which is a public good?
qs.why: Streetlights serve everyone and use by one does not reduce use by others.

qs.q: Pollution from a factory is an example of a negative externality.
qs.why: People nearby bear a cost they did not agree to.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
pairs: Open to all, use does not exclude others

qs.q: Order markets by number of sellers, fewest to most

learn.b: GDP, gross domestic product, is the total value of final goods and services made in a country in a period. It measures the size of an economy. It counts new production, not used items resold.
Nominal GDP uses current prices. Real GDP adjusts for inflation so you can compare years fairly. If prices rise 5% and output is the same, nominal GDP grows but real GDP does not.
The economy goes through ups and downs. Expansion is growth, a peak is the high point, contraction is decline, and a trough is the low point. A recession is a significant fall in economic activity.

qs.q: What does GDP measure?
o: Total value of final goods and services produced
qs.why: GDP is the value of final output in a period.

qs.q: What does real GDP adjust for?
qs.why: Real GDP removes the effect of price changes.

qs.q: Which counts in GDP for this year?
o: A new car built and sold this year
qs.why: GDP counts newly produced final goods.

qs.q: What is a recession?
o: A significant decline in economic activity
qs.why: Recessions involve falling output, jobs and income.

qs.q: GDP counts the resale of used goods.
qs.why: Only newly produced goods and services count.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
pairs: Value of goods and services made

qs.q: Put the business cycle phases in order starting from growth

learn.b: Inflation is a general rise in prices over time. The CPI, consumer price index, tracks the price of a typical basket of goods people buy. If CPI rises 3%, prices are about 3% higher.
Deflation is when prices fall over time. It sounds nice but can make people delay buying, which hurts the economy. Most central banks aim for low, stable inflation.
The labor force is people who have a job or are actively looking. The unemployment rate is the percent of the labor force without a job. A student not looking for work is not counted as unemployed.

qs.q: What does CPI measure?
o: Average price changes of a basket of consumer goods
qs.why: CPI tracks the cost of a typical shopping basket.

qs.q: What is the unemployment rate?
o: People without a job divided by population
Percent of the labor force without a job who are looking
qs.why: It uses the labor force as the base.

qs.q: What is deflation?
qs.why: Deflation is a decline in the price level.

qs.q: Who is counted as unemployed?
o: A full-time student not looking for work
Someone without a job who is actively looking
qs.why: Unemployed means jobless and actively seeking work.

qs.q: Inflation reduces the purchasing power of money.
qs.why: When prices rise, each dollar buys less.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
Order these yearly price changes from lowest to highest

learn.b: Fiscal policy is how the government uses taxes and spending to influence the economy. Cutting taxes or spending more can boost growth. A budget deficit happens when spending is higher than revenue.
Monetary policy is run by the central bank, like the Federal Reserve in the US. It sets interest rates and influences the money supply. Lower rates make borrowing cheaper.
When prices rise too fast, a central bank may raise interest rates. Borrowing becomes costlier and spending slows. This eases pressure on prices.

qs.q: What is fiscal policy?
o: Setting interest rates by a central bank
qs.why: Fiscal policy uses the government budget.

qs.q: Who runs monetary policy in the US?
qs.why: The Federal Reserve is the US central bank.

qs.q: If a central bank raises interest rates, what generally happens to borrowing?
qs.why: Higher rates raise the cost of loans.

qs.q: What is a budget deficit?
qs.why: A deficit means the government spends more than it collects.

qs.q: Fiscal policy is set by the central bank.
qs.why: Fiscal policy is set by government; the central bank handles monetary policy.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
Order how a rate hike cools inflation

learn.b: Exports are goods and services sold to other countries. Imports are those bought from other countries. Trade lets countries get things they cannot make cheaply.
A country has a comparative advantage when it can make something at a lower opportunity cost than others. Each country does best by specializing in what it makes most efficiently, then trading.
A tariff is a tax on imported goods. An exchange rate is the price of one currency in another. If a currency gets stronger, imports for that country become cheaper.

qs.q: What are exports?
o: Goods and services sold to other countries
qs.why: Exports leave the country to be sold abroad.

qs.q: What is a tariff?
qs.why: Tariffs raise the price of imports.

qs.q: What is comparative advantage?
o: Making something at a lower opportunity cost
qs.why: It is about lower opportunity cost, not absolute output.

qs.q: If a country's currency strengthens, imports generally become what?
qs.why: A stronger currency buys more foreign goods.

qs.q: Countries can both gain from trade by specializing where their opportunity cost is lower.
qs.why: Specialization and trade can raise total output for both.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
pairs: Price of one currency in another

qs.q: Put a trade chain in order

learn.b: A business makes goods, like shoes, or provides services, like haircuts, to earn money. It exists to meet customer needs. Some businesses sell both.
Revenue is the money from sales. Expenses are the costs of running the business. Profit is revenue minus expenses.
Stakeholders are people affected by a business: owners, employees, customers, suppliers and the community. Good businesses think about all of them.

qs.q: What is revenue?
qs.why: Revenue is the total sales income.

qs.q: How is profit calculated?
qs.why: Profit is what remains after expenses.

qs.q: Which is a service?
qs.why: Services are actions done for customers, not physical items.

qs.q: Who is a stakeholder of a business?
qs.why: Employees, customers, suppliers and owners are all affected.

qs.q: A business always makes a profit.
qs.why: If expenses exceed revenue, a business has a loss.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
Put the steps of running a lemonade stand in order

learn.b: A sole proprietorship has one owner who keeps all profit and is personally responsible for debts. A partnership has two or more owners who share profit and responsibility.
An LLC, limited liability company, is a flexible structure. In general it keeps owners' personal belongings separate from business debts. This is called limited liability.
A corporation is a separate legal entity owned by shareholders. It can raise money by selling shares. It is more complex and has more rules.

qs.q: How many owners does a sole proprietorship have?
qs.why: Sole means one owner.

qs.q: What does limited liability mean?
o: Owners are generally not personally responsible for all business debts
qs.why: Personal assets are generally protected from business debts.

qs.q: What is a corporation?
o: A separate legal entity owned by shareholders
qs.why: A corporation is legally separate from its owners.

qs.q: How many owners does a partnership have?
qs.why: Partnerships are owned by two or more people.

qs.q: An LLC can generally protect owners' personal assets from business debts.
qs.why: Limited liability is the main feature of an LLC.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
Put the steps of forming a company in order

learn.b: A supply chain is the path from raw materials to the customer. Inventory is the goods a business holds for sale. Too little means lost sales, too much ties up money.
Managers plan (set goals), organize (arrange people and resources), lead (guide and motivate) and control (check results and fix problems).
SWOT stands for Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities and Threats. Strengths and weaknesses are inside the business. Opportunities and threats come from outside, like new rivals.

qs.q: What is a supply chain?
o: The path from raw materials to the customer
qs.why: It covers everything needed to get a product to buyers.

qs.q: What is inventory?
o: Goods a business holds for sale
qs.why: Inventory is the stock of goods ready to sell.

qs.q: What does the T in SWOT stand for?
qs.why: SWOT is Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, Threats.

qs.q: Which management function means setting goals and deciding how to reach them?
qs.why: Planning sets the goals and the path.

qs.q: Opportunities and threats in a SWOT analysis are internal to the company.
qs.why: They are external; strengths and weaknesses are internal.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
Put the management functions in order

learn.b: Cash flow is the movement of money in and out of a business. Positive cash flow means more comes in than goes out. A profitable business can still run out of cash if customers pay late.
The break-even point is when revenue equals total costs, so profit is zero. Economies of scale mean the cost per unit falls as a business makes more.
Products go through introduction, growth, maturity and decline. Business ethics means doing the right thing, such as honest ads and fair pay. Trust helps a business last.

qs.q: What is cash flow?
o: Movement of money in and out
qs.why: Cash flow tracks money entering and leaving.

qs.q: What are economies of scale?
o: Cost per unit falls as output grows
qs.why: Making more can spread costs and lower the unit cost.

qs.q: What is the break-even point?
qs.why: At break-even, profit is zero.

qs.q: Which is the first stage of the product life cycle?
qs.why: A product starts with its introduction to the market.

qs.q: A profitable business can still run out of cash.
qs.why: Timing matters: if money arrives late, bills may go unpaid.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
pairs: Lower unit cost with more output

qs.q: Put the product life cycle in order

learn.b: An entrepreneur starts and runs a business and takes on financial risk. Many great businesses begin by solving a real problem. Example: a tutoring app for students who need homework help.
Your target market is the group of people you want to serve. Market research means collecting information about customers and competitors, by talking to people or using surveys.
A value proposition explains why customers should choose you. It answers: what problem do you solve and why are you better? Keep it short and clear.

qs.q: What is an entrepreneur?
o: Someone who only works for others
Someone who starts and runs a business and takes risk
qs.why: Entrepreneurs create businesses and accept financial risk.

qs.q: Good business ideas often do what?
o: Solve a real problem for customers
qs.why: Solving a problem gives people a reason to buy.

qs.q: What is a value proposition?
o: The reason customers should choose your product
qs.why: It states the benefit you offer.

qs.q: What is market research?
o: Collecting information about customers and competitors
qs.why: Research helps you understand the market before you spend.

qs.q: Talking to potential customers before launching can reduce risk.
qs.why: You learn what people want before investing heavily.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
Put the steps of developing an idea in order

learn.b: A business plan is a written plan of your goals and how to reach them. An MVP, minimum viable product, is the simplest version you can test with real customers. It saves time and money.
Startup costs are what you must spend before earning, such as equipment, a website and licenses. Estimate them to know how much money you need.

Bootstrapping uses your own savings and sales. A loan must be repaid with interest but you keep ownership. Equity investors give money for a share of ownership. Crowdfunding collects small sums from many people.

qs.q: What is an MVP?
o: The simplest version you can test with customers
qs.why: An MVP tests the idea with minimal effort.

qs.q: What is bootstrapping?
o: Funding a business with your own savings and sales
qs.why: Bootstrapped founders rely on their own money.

qs.q: What does an equity investor receive?
qs.why: Equity means ownership in the company.

qs.q: What is a business plan?
o: A written plan of goals and how to reach them
qs.why: It lays out the idea, market, costs and goals.

qs.q: A loan gives the lender part ownership of your business.
qs.why: A loan is repaid with interest; it does not give ownership.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
Put the startup steps in order

learn.b: Cost-plus pricing means cost plus a markup. If a product costs $6 and you add a 50% markup, the price is $9. Prices that are too low can cause losses, and too high can scare customers away.
Break-even is when revenue equals costs. If fixed costs are $100 and each sale adds $5 after variable costs, you need 20 sales to break even.
Customer feedback shows what to improve. A pivot is a big change in strategy based on what you learn. Scaling means growing without costs rising as fast as sales.

qs.q: A product costs $6 to make. With a 50% markup on cost, what is the price?
Fixed costs are $100 and each sale adds $5 toward them. How many sales to break even?
What is a pivot?
o: A change in strategy based on what you learn
qs.why: Startups pivot when evidence shows a better path.

qs.q: What does scaling mean?
o: Growing without costs rising as fast as sales
qs.why: Scaling grows revenue faster than costs.

qs.q: A price that is too low can never hurt a business.
qs.why: Very low prices can fail to cover costs and cause losses.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
Put the growth stages in order

learn.b: Good leaders share a clear goal and delegate, which means giving tasks to others. They also listen. Setbacks are normal, and smart founders learn from them.
Intellectual property protects creations. A patent protects an invention. A trademark protects a name or logo. A copyright protects creative works like writing and music.
Ethics means honest ads, fair pay and respecting customers. Trust helps a business grow over time.

qs.q: What does a trademark protect?
qs.why: Trademarks protect identifiers of a brand.

qs.q: What does a patent protect?
qs.why: Patents cover new inventions.

qs.q: What does a copyright protect?
o: Creative works like writing or music
qs.why: Copyright covers original creative works.

qs.q: What does delegation mean?
qs.why: Delegating shares work with team members.

qs.q: A trademark can protect a brand logo.
qs.why: Logos are a classic trademark use.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
Put the steps of learning from a setback in order

learn.b: Marketing is everything a business does to understand customers and get them interested in its products. Advertising is only one part.
The 4 Ps are Product (what you sell), Price (what it costs), Place (where it is sold) and Promotion (how you tell people). Together they form a marketing mix.
No product suits everyone. A target market is the group you aim at. Segmentation divides people by age, interests or needs so you can speak to them directly.

qs.q: Which are the 4 Ps of marketing?
qs.why: The marketing mix is product, price, place and promotion.

qs.q: Which P describes where a product is sold?
qs.why: Place covers where and how customers can buy.

qs.q: What is a target market?
o: The group of customers a business aims at
qs.why: Businesses focus on the people most likely to buy.

qs.q: What is segmentation?
o: Dividing a market into groups with similar traits
qs.why: Segments help tailor messages to groups.

qs.q: Marketing means only advertising.
qs.why: Marketing also includes research, pricing, product design and distribution.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
Put the marketing planning steps in order

learn.b: A brand is the identity and feeling people connect with a business. It includes the name, logo, colors and promises. A strong brand is easy to remember.
A USP, unique selling proposition, is what makes you different from others. Positioning is the place your brand holds in customers' minds compared with competitors.
Brand voice is the personality in your words, like friendly or serious. Using the same voice and look everywhere builds trust and recognition.

qs.q: What is a brand?
o: The identity and feeling people connect with a business
qs.why: A brand is more than a logo; it is the whole impression.

qs.q: What does USP stand for?
qs.why: A USP is what makes you different.

qs.q: What is positioning?
o: Your brand's place in customers' minds versus rivals
qs.why: Positioning is about perception relative to competitors.

qs.q: What is brand voice?
o: The personality of a brand's words
qs.why: Voice shows personality in how a brand communicates.

qs.q: Consistent branding helps customers recognize a business.
qs.why: Repetition builds familiarity and trust.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
Put the steps of building a brand in order

learn.b: SEO, search engine optimization, means improving your website so it shows higher in search results without paying for ads. Content marketing means sharing useful posts or videos to attract customers.
Social media lets brands talk with people directly. Email reaches people who already signed up. A CTA, call to action, tells people what to do next, like Sign up now.
A conversion happens when a visitor does what you wanted, such as buying. CTR, click-through rate, is the percent of viewers who click. If 1,000 people see an ad and 50 click, CTR is 5%.

qs.q: What does SEO try to do?
o: Help a website rank higher in search results
qs.why: SEO improves organic visibility.

qs.q: What is a CTA?
o: A prompt telling people what to do next
qs.why: CTA means call to action.

qs.q: An ad is seen 1,000 times and clicked 50 times. What is the CTR?
What is a conversion?
o: A visitor taking the desired action
qs.why: A conversion is a completed goal like a purchase or sign-up.

qs.q: SEO means paying for search ads.
qs.why: SEO is about earning higher results unpaid, not buying ads.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
Put the customer journey in order

learn.b: A survey asks people for opinions. An A/B test shows two versions, like two ad headlines, to different groups and compares which works better.
Retention means keeping existing customers buying. Customer acquisition cost is how much it costs to win a new customer. Keeping a customer is often cheaper than finding a new one.
Ads should not make false claims. Misleading customers can break the law and harms trust. Ethical marketing respects privacy and tells the truth.

qs.q: What is an A/B test?
o: Comparing two versions to see which performs better
qs.why: A/B tests compare two options with real audiences.

qs.q: What is customer retention?
qs.why: Retention is about repeat business.

qs.q: What is a survey?
qs.why: Surveys gather customer feedback.

qs.q: Why is false advertising a problem?
o: It is unethical and can be illegal
qs.why: Misleading claims harm customers and break trust.

qs.q: Keeping an existing customer is often cheaper than winning a new one.
qs.why: New customers usually require more marketing spend.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
pairs: Cost to win a new customer

qs.q: Put the steps of an A/B test in order

learn.b: Accounting records, summarizes and reports a business's money. Bookkeeping is the day-to-day recording of transactions. Owners, banks and tax offices use the reports.
Assets are things the business owns, like cash and equipment. Liabilities are what it owes, like loans. Equity is the owner's share after debts are paid.
Assets = Liabilities + Equity. This always balances. If assets are $500 and liabilities are $200, equity is $300.

qs.q: What is the accounting equation?
qs.why: The two sides of the balance sheet must always match.

qs.q: Which is an asset?
qs.why: Assets are resources owned by the business.

qs.q: Which is a liability?
qs.why: Liabilities are amounts the business owes.

qs.q: What is bookkeeping?
qs.why: Bookkeepers keep daily financial records.

qs.q: If assets are $500 and liabilities are $200, equity is $300.
Match each term to its meaning
Put the basic accounting steps in order

learn.b: In double-entry bookkeeping, every transaction affects at least two accounts. Total debits always equal total credits. This helps catch mistakes.
A debit is an entry on the left side of an account. A credit is on the right. Debits increase assets and expenses. Credits increase liabilities, equity and revenue.
The journal records transactions in date order. The ledger groups them by account. If you pay cash for equipment, equipment goes up and cash goes down.

qs.q: What does double-entry mean?
o: Every transaction is recorded twice in different books only
Every transaction affects at least two accounts
qs.why: Each transaction has a debit side and a credit side.

qs.q: Which side increases an asset account?
qs.why: Debits increase asset accounts.

qs.q: A business pays cash for new equipment. What changes?
o: Equipment goes up and cash goes down
qs.why: One asset rises while another asset falls.

qs.q: What is a ledger?
qs.why: The ledger organizes transactions by account.

qs.q: A debit always means a decrease.
qs.why: Debits increase assets and expenses, and decrease liabilities.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
Put the recording steps in order

learn.b: The income statement shows revenue, expenses and profit over a period, like a month. Net income = revenue - expenses. Example: $500 revenue and $350 expenses leaves $150.
The balance sheet is a snapshot of assets, liabilities and equity on one date. It shows what the business owns and owes at that moment.
The cash flow statement shows cash coming in and going out. A business can show profit but still lack cash. Owners check all three statements.

qs.q: What does an income statement show?
o: Revenue, expenses and profit over a period
qs.why: It covers performance across a period.

qs.q: What does a balance sheet show?
o: Assets, liabilities and equity at a point in time
qs.why: It is a snapshot at a specific date.

qs.q: Revenue is $500 and expenses are $350. What is net income?
What does a cash flow statement show?
o: Cash coming in and going out
qs.why: It tracks cash movements.

qs.q: A balance sheet is a snapshot at one date.
qs.why: It reports balances at a specific point in time.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
pairs: Snapshot of what is owned and owed

qs.q: Put these income statement lines in order from top to bottom

learn.b: Gross profit = revenue - cost of goods sold. The current ratio = current assets / current liabilities. If you have $200 of current assets and $100 of current liabilities, it is 2.
Depreciation spreads the cost of an asset, like a machine, over its useful life. A $1,000 machine lasting 5 years can be recorded as $200 of expense per year.
Accrual accounting records revenue when earned and expenses when incurred, even if cash moves later. Cash-basis records when cash moves. An audit is an independent check of financial records.

qs.q: How is gross profit calculated?
o: Revenue minus cost of goods sold
qs.why: Gross profit is sales minus direct production cost.

qs.q: Current assets are $200 and current liabilities are $100. What is the current ratio?
What does depreciation do?
o: Spreads an asset's cost over its useful life
qs.why: It matches an asset's cost to the years it is used.

qs.q: When does accrual accounting record revenue?
qs.why: Accrual records revenue when earned, not when paid.

qs.q: Under cash-basis accounting, revenue is recorded when the sale is made even if unpaid.
qs.why: Cash-basis records revenue when cash is actually received.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
Put these profit lines in order from top to bottom

learn.b: Residential property is for living, like houses and apartments. Commercial property is for business, like offices and shops. Land can be used for either or kept as it is.
Renters pay a landlord and do not build ownership. Owners pay for upkeep, taxes and often a mortgage, but build equity. Equity is the home's value minus the loan still owed.
Appreciation is when a property's value rises over time. Values can also fall. Location, demand and the economy all matter.

qs.q: What is residential property?
o: Property meant for people to live in
qs.why: Residential means homes where people live.

qs.q: How is home equity calculated?
qs.why: Equity is your ownership share after the loan.

qs.q: What is appreciation?
o: A rise in a property's value
qs.why: Appreciation means value goes up over time.

qs.q: Who does a renter pay?
qs.why: Rent is paid to the property owner or landlord.

qs.q: Renting a home builds ownership equity.
qs.why: Rent payments do not give the renter ownership of the property.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
Put the steps of renting a home in order

learn.b: A mortgage is a loan used to buy property. The property is collateral. If payments stop, the lender can take the property in a process called foreclosure.
A down payment is the part of the price you pay up front in cash. On a $200,000 home, a 10% down payment is $20,000. The rest is borrowed. Principal is the amount borrowed.
A fixed-rate mortgage keeps the same interest rate for its whole term. An adjustable-rate mortgage can change over time. Amortization is paying off the loan gradually through regular payments.

qs.q: What is a down payment?
o: Money paid up front toward the price
qs.why: It is the cash you pay at the start of the purchase.

qs.q: A home costs $200,000. How much is a 10% down payment?
What does a fixed-rate mortgage mean?
o: The price of the house is fixed
The interest rate stays the same for the term
qs.why: A fixed rate does not change over the term.

qs.q: What secures a mortgage loan?
qs.why: The home acts as collateral for the lender.

qs.q: If you stop paying a mortgage, the lender may take the property through foreclosure.
qs.why: Foreclosure lets the lender recover money by taking the property.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
Put the path to buying with a mortgage in order

learn.b: An inspection checks the condition of the home. An appraisal estimates its market value, and lenders use it to decide how much they will lend.
Closing costs are fees paid when the sale is finished. Owners also pay property tax to local government, homeowner insurance and maintenance. These are on top of the mortgage.
Escrow is when a neutral third party holds money or documents until all conditions of the deal are met. Many lenders also collect taxes and insurance through an escrow account.

qs.q: What does a home inspection do?
o: Examines the condition of the home
qs.why: Inspectors look for problems in the building.

qs.q: What is an appraisal?
o: An estimate of a property's value
qs.why: Appraisers estimate market value.

qs.q: What are closing costs?
o: The cost of closing a bank account
Fees paid when the purchase is completed
qs.why: They cover loan, legal and other fees at closing.

qs.q: Who receives property tax?
qs.why: Property tax funds local services.

qs.q: An appraisal is a monthly loan payment.
qs.why: An appraisal is an estimate of value, not a payment.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
Put the buying steps in order

learn.b: Owners can rent property to earn income. Cash flow from a rental is rent minus costs such as the mortgage, taxes, insurance and repairs. Vacancy, when no one is renting, means lost income.
Leverage means using borrowed money to buy an asset. It can magnify gains, but it also magnifies losses. Debt still must be repaid if the property falls in value.
A REIT is a company that owns income-producing real estate, and you can buy its shares like a stock. Real estate is illiquid, meaning it can take time to sell and turn into cash.

qs.q: What is a REIT?
o: A company that owns income-producing real estate with shares you can buy
qs.why: REITs let people invest in real estate through shares.

qs.q: How is rental cash flow calculated?
qs.why: Cash flow is income left after costs.

qs.q: What does illiquid mean?
o: Easy to sell in a second
Slow and harder to turn into cash
qs.why: Real estate can take weeks or months to sell.

qs.q: What is vacancy?
o: A period when a unit is empty and earns no rent
qs.why: Empty units do not produce rental income.

qs.q: Using borrowed money to buy property is called leverage and can magnify both gains and losses.
qs.why: Debt amplifies results in both directions.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
Put the steps to find rental cash flow in order

learn.b: Governments collect taxes to pay for public services like roads, schools and emergency help. Common taxes include income tax, sales tax and property tax.
Gross pay is what you earn before anything is taken out. Net pay, or take-home pay, is what you receive after taxes and other deductions. Employers withhold tax from each paycheck.
A tax return is a form that reports your income and works out your tax. If too much was withheld, you get a refund. If too little, you owe more.

qs.q: What are taxes mainly used for?
o: Public services like roads and schools
qs.why: Tax revenue funds services for the public.

qs.q: What is gross pay?
qs.why: Gross pay is total earnings before anything is taken out.

qs.q: What is withholding?
o: An employer taking tax out of your paycheck
qs.why: Employers withhold tax and send it to the government.

qs.q: What is a tax return?
o: A form reporting income and calculating tax owed or refunded
qs.why: It summarizes your income and tax for the year.

qs.q: Your take-home pay is the same as your gross pay.
qs.why: Take-home pay is lower because taxes are taken out.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
Put the pay and tax cycle in order

learn.b: Many income taxes are progressive: higher income is taxed at higher rates. Income is split into tax brackets, and each slice is taxed at its own rate.
The marginal rate is the rate on your next dollar earned. The effective rate is your total tax divided by your total income. The effective rate is usually lower than the top bracket you reach.
Taxable income is your income minus deductions. Only this amount is run through the brackets. Moving into a higher bracket taxes only the income above that threshold at the higher rate.

qs.q: What is a progressive tax?
o: Higher incomes are taxed at higher rates
qs.why: Progressive taxes rise in rate as income rises.

qs.q: What is a marginal tax rate?
o: The rate on your next dollar of income
qs.why: Marginal rate applies to additional income.

qs.q: How is taxable income calculated?
qs.why: Deductions reduce the amount that is taxed.

qs.q: What is the effective tax rate?
o: Total tax divided by total income
qs.why: It shows the overall percentage of income paid in tax.

qs.q: Moving into a higher bracket does not tax all your income at the higher rate.
qs.why: Only the portion above the threshold is taxed at the higher rate.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
Put the steps of calculating income tax in order

learn.b: A deduction lowers your taxable income. If you are in a 20% bracket, a $1,000 deduction saves about $200 in tax. The standard deduction is a fixed amount you can subtract without listing expenses.
A tax credit lowers your tax bill directly, dollar for dollar. A $1,000 credit cuts your tax by $1,000. That makes a credit usually worth more than a deduction of the same size.
Itemizing means listing eligible expenses, like certain interest or charity gifts. You normally choose whichever method gives the larger deduction.

qs.q: What does a tax deduction reduce?
qs.why: Deductions lower the income that is taxed.

qs.q: What does a tax credit reduce?
o: Your tax bill dollar for dollar
qs.why: Credits subtract directly from tax owed.

qs.q: Which usually lowers tax more: a $1,000 credit or a $1,000 deduction?
qs.why: A credit reduces tax by $1,000; a deduction only saves tax at your rate.

qs.q: What is a standard deduction?
o: A fixed amount you can subtract without listing expenses
qs.why: It is a flat deduction available to most filers.

qs.q: A tax credit only reduces taxable income.
qs.why: A credit reduces the tax owed directly, not the income.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
Put the steps for choosing a deduction method in order

learn.b: An employee works for an employer. The employer withholds income tax and payroll taxes from each paycheck and sends you a W-2 form at year end. You give a W-4 form to set how much is withheld.

An independent contractor, or freelancer, is paid without withholding and usually gets a 1099 form. They must set aside money for their own taxes and often make estimated tax payments during the year.
Employees share Social Security and Medicare taxes with their employer. Self-employed people pay both parts, called self-employment tax. Keeping good records of income and expenses is important.

qs.q: Which form do employees usually receive at year end?
qs.why: A W-2 reports wages and tax withheld.

qs.q: Who handles tax payments for a 1099 contractor?
qs.why: Contractors are responsible for their own taxes.

qs.q: What does Form W-4 do?
o: Tells an employer how much tax to withhold
qs.why: The W-4 sets withholding for an employee's paycheck.

qs.q: What does self-employment tax cover?
o: Social Security and Medicare for self-employed people
qs.why: It funds Social Security and Medicare contributions of the self-employed.

qs.q: Independent contractors generally must set aside money for their own taxes.
qs.why: No employer withholds tax from their payments.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
pairs: Payments by the self-employed during the year

qs.q: Put a freelancer's tax cycle in order
